overview.summary: Entrepreneurs start and run businesses, taking an idea for a product or service and trying to turn it into something people will pay for.
overview.problems: They look for problems that customers have and build ways to solve them.
overview.worksWith: Customers, suppliers, early team members, advisers, banks and sometimes investors.
overview.workplaces: Home offices, shared workspaces, shops, workshops and online. The setting depends on the kind of business.

timeline.title: Check the numbers and set priorities
timeline.description: The entrepreneur looks at money coming in and going out, orders or sign-ups, and chooses the one or two most important tasks for the day.
timeline.why: Small businesses can run into trouble when cash runs short, so tracking the basics matters.

timeline.title: Talk to customers
timeline.description: Calls, messages or visits help the entrepreneur understand what customers need, what they dislike and what they would pay for.
timeline.why: An idea only becomes useful when it solves a problem real people have.

timeline.title: Build or improve the product or service
timeline.description: The entrepreneur makes something, improves it or delivers orders. In the early days they often do this work themselves.
timeline.why: The offer has to work well before anyone will recommend it.

timeline.title: Sales and marketing
timeline.description: Replying to enquiries, posting updates, contacting possible customers and negotiating with suppliers.
timeline.why: Without customers there is no business.

timeline.title: Admin, legal and money tasks
timeline.description: Sending invoices, paying bills, keeping records and handling licences and taxes.
timeline.why: Rules and records protect the business and its owner.

timeline.title: Review and learn
timeline.description: The entrepreneur notes what worked and what did not, and decides what small experiment to try next.
timeline.why: Small experiments reduce risk and speed up learning.

responsibilities: Finding a problem worth solving and deciding what to build
Deciding what to stop doing as well as what to start
Selling and acting on customer feedback
Hiring and leading other people as the business grows
challenges: Income can be irregular, especially in the early period.
Many new businesses struggle or close, so planning for risk matters.
One person often has to do many different jobs at once.
Big decisions can feel lonely and stressful.
Work and personal life can blur together.
Rejection from customers or funders is common and has to be handled calmly.
workEnvironment: It varies from a home desk or shared office to a shop, workshop or fully online work. Hours are often long and flexible, and weekends are common in the early stages.
rewards: The chance to create value and, later, jobs for others
tradeoffs: Responsibility for everything that goes wrong
Results depend partly on timing and circumstances outside your control

activity.title: Run a mini customer interview
steps: Notice a small problem among classmates or family, for example finding a quiet place to study.
Write five open questions, such as how people solve the problem now and what they dislike about it.
With their permission, ask three to five people and write down their answers.
Look for a pattern: which problem was mentioned most?
Write one sentence about a possible solution and one cheap way to test it.
activity.outcome: You practise talking to possible customers and testing an idea before spending any money.
activity.safety: Ask only with permission, do not collect private or sensitive details, and do not spend money or make promises to others.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
